source.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
source.authors: Moghis Fereidouni; Muhammad Umair Haider; Peizhong Ju; A. Siddique

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure values are not given numerically in the text and are recorded only where the authors state them explicitly.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures concept overlap and activation-distribution separability in language-model neurons and SAE features, using metrics different from the original neuron visualizations.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports concept-erasure intervention results. Those evaluate the performance of particular interventions, not the frequency or separability of polysemantic neurons, so they are not recorded as rows for these claim versions. Cited findings from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures salient-unit overlap across concept classes in Gemma-2-2B (and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B), which bears on V2. It also argues, using activation-distribution plots, that units shared across concepts can still separate them, which bears on V7. The units are hidden-state (residual-stream) dimensions, not MLP neurons. The main comparison is base hidden dimensions against SAE latents, a post-hoc decomposition rather than a change to the model's architecture or training, so it does not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs reduce but do not eliminate polysemanticity and give higher JS concept separability than base models, in both Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek. Wider SAEs, and sparser SAEs at equal width, are more separable. Distribution-aware measures capture distinctions that binary overlap misses. SAEs enable more precise partial concept erasure, and their APP method has the smallest perplexity cost.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates concept-labelled activation overlap and Jensen–Shannon distances across language-model and SAE representations, rather than using the original visual neuron-interpretation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with representation (base versus SAE), SAE width and l0 sparsity, dataset, and the measurement choice: top-80 salient-neuron overlap, all-active-SAE-neuron overlap, or activation-distribution separability.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE latents show lower top-80 salient overlap than base hidden dimensions (POS about 38% to about 18%). They also show higher JS separability on all five datasets (e.g. DBpedia 0.405 to 0.621/0.680). Polysemantic latents remain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE decompositions reduce, but do not eliminate, polysemanticity relative to base-model units.

fits_no_version.finding: Wider SAEs (65k) are more separable and have less overlap than 16k SAEs. At the same width, lower l0 gives higher separability (Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latent monosemanticity increases with dictionary width and sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: Layer JS separability correlates with concept-erasure precision: r=0.771 for partial methods and r=0.657 for full masking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distribution separability of units predicts how selectively a concept can be erased.

record.code_released: Code will be released publicly after paper acceptance; no URL is stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The main overlap comparison is based on the top 80 salient neurons per concept, and the authors describe that analysis as limited in scope. The separability scores are layer-level averages and do not directly report the proportion of individual neurons that are polysemantic. The paper says quantitative concept-erasure table results are from a single representative run; selected repeated runs are mentioned, but no uncertainty estimates are reported for the separability scores.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Figure-only values without explicit textual numbers were not transcribed as numerical results.

untested.parts: MLP neurons specifically: only hidden-state dimensions are analysed. Variation across layers is not reported. Concepts are labelled classes, not unrelated tokens or contexts.
The superposition cause is not tested. The SAE-width remarks are interpretation only.
Initialization, regularization and training-noise causes are not tested.
No change to the LM's activation function, architecture or regularization. SAE vs base compares a decomposition, not a retrained model.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
Explanation-scoring procedures are not varied. There is no quantitative count of units reclassified under the overlap vs JS views.

missing.what: Neuron-level activation-distribution plots showing units shared across concepts but with overlapping vs separable distributions. This is the basis of the V7 verdict.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B base JS separability scores (0.367, 0.291, 0.436, 0.325, 0.366), but these cannot show the share of polysemantic units.
Appendix H: highly separable base neuron 1621 still shifts toward a secondary topic on mixed sentences. Authors call this polysemantic encoding.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 links and V5 supports label are dropped. Comparing SAE latents with base dimensions is not a change to the LM's activation function, architecture or regularization. 'Neurons' in the base model are hidden-state (residual-stream) components; interventions are placed after the MLP plus residual in the final block. They are therefore not MLP neurons, which weakens the fit to V2. Base JS scores are layer means without a threshold and cannot give a share.

versions.untested_parts: Image classifiers, InceptionV1, and the cited cat-face/car-front example are not studied.
The study uses concept-labelled datasets, not an analysis of unrelated tokens or contexts as such. It does not report how polysemanticity varies by transformer layer.

The study compares SAE widths and describes greater capacity as allowing more distinct concept assignments, but does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than the network has neurons.
Initialization, regularization or training noise as causes of polysemanticity when there is sufficient neuron capacity are not tested.

The study compares base representations with SAE variants and compares SAE widths and sparsity levels. It does not test SoLU, modern convnets, or activation-function changes. Its concept-erasure perplexity results are not a direct test of the performance cost of reducing polysemanticity.
The study does not investigate canonical mixed-selectivity neurons to determine whether unrelated inputs share one underlying feature or job.
The study compares salient-neuron overlap, activation-distribution separability and an all-active-SAE-neuron overlap analysis. It does not vary explanation-scoring procedures.

relation.reason: Results on polysemanticity in LMs bear on V2.

tranche.reason: Different method (salient overlap and JS separability) on the same question.

source_check.notes: Sec 3.1 overlap is IoU of the top-80 sets, so '38% of top 80 per concept' follows the authors' loose wording. The analysis layer is not stated (interventions are at the final-block residual output). The text says code comes after acceptance and gives no link. App H calls the separable Fig 2 neurons polysemantic.

statements.correction: Sec 1, Sec 3.2, Fig 2/5: binary overlap counts units as shared even when their concept-conditioned distributions can separate; authors say such units may still count as monosemantic. App E: all-active overlap computed for SAEs only (base neurons all active, so uninformative); 65k below 16k, consistent with top-80. No share of polysemantic units is compared across definitions.
statements.problem: The study does not report results that differ across the three measures. Top-80 overlap, all-active SAE overlap and JS separability all agree: SAEs are below base, and 65k is below 16k. Appendix E calls the all-active result consistent with Fig 1.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2B base model compared with 16k and 65k SAE variants on five datasets
reader_labels.reason: The reported separability scores are higher for both SAE widths than for the base model in each dataset, with the 65k SAE exceeding the 16k SAE in each Table 1 comparison (R4-R18).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The study reports overlap-based results alongside a distribution-aware JS score, and explains that neurons shared across concepts can have either overlapping or clearly separated activation distributions (R1-R18).
